doc.title: Evan Christopher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 1, 2009

chapter: Coming to New Orleans and the clarinet tradition
title: The New Orleans clarinet niche and the missing teachers in 1994
summary: The niche revealed itself: no clarinetists were left to study with when he arrived in 1994, Willie Humphrey having just died. He had not yet met Kenny Davern or discovered the Creole clarinets of the Caribbean.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: This New Orleans clarinet tradition. I would have to guess this was not something that you sat down and said where’s a niche for me, and then recognized this niche and pursued it.

No the niche revealed itself. The niche revealed itself. Because you have to remember, Monk, when I actually moved to New Orleans in 1994, there were no clarinetists left for me to study with directly. Willie Humphrey would have been the last and he passed away just months before my arrival to the city. So it’s not that the style revealed itself to me as my niche, it’s just that I kept finding it strange that the only clarinetists that I enjoy were gone, were in recordings, I mean in New Orleans proper. And of course this was also a year before I met Kenny Davern, so this was a year before I’d spent time in New Orleans, working in New Orleans, realizing that the language of the clarinet had style-specific elements that are what made it so special and unique. This was before, this was a couple of years before I discovered the Creole clarinets of the Caribbean, of Martinique and the French West Indies. So there was a lot of vocabulary that I hadn’t really gotten to yet,
even when I first moved to New Orleans there was a lot of vocabulary I didn’t — that had captured my ear enough to check it out, but I hadn’t really incorporated it.
